title: Have you noticed yet?
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman argues that while opponents of the science of learning chase a distraction, a more seismic shift is taking place in Australian education: the review of the Australian Professional Standards for Teachers. He notes that the current standards are vague, tell teachers to know how students learn without saying what the research is, and have even been used by some training providers to block placements at schools requiring shared lesson plans. The new discussion paper from AITSL, by contrast, endorses sequencing from simple to complex, building on prior knowledge, explicit instruction, modelling, cognitive load management and strong formative assessment, and it backs teaching required behaviours with routines. What Ashman finds most personally validating is that the paper questions the term differentiation and endorses whole-class teaching with tiered interventions. He observes that a systematic review of differentiation by its own advocates found no positive evidence, so attention has moved to multi-tiered systems of support. He predicts the mention of cognitive science will provoke a backlash and urges readers to take part in the consultation.
points: The current standards require teachers to know how students learn but say nothing about what that research actually is, while the discussion paper names specific evidence on sequencing, explicit instruction and cognitive load.
The paper is strong on formative assessment and on teaching required behaviours through routines and acting when expectations are not met.
It questions the term differentiation as lacking a consistent definition and points toward whole-class teaching alongside tiered interventions, a position Ashman has argued for years.
A systematic review of differentiation by its own advocates found no positive evidence, so the field has quietly shifted to multi-tiered systems of support, which are better defined.
Ashman expects the explicit reference to cognitive science to trigger accusations of positivism and urges teachers to respond to the consultation.
quotes: The current standards require teachers to ‘know students and how they learn’ but they say nothing specific about how students learn.

Evidence shows learning is strengthened when teachers sequence content from simple to complex, build on prior knowledge, and use explicit instruction, modelling and guided application of new learning.

Learning is further enhanced when instructional materials are designed to manage cognitive load, focus attention on key information, and effectively integrate visual, verbal and written representations.

This is marvellous to read, but the most personally validating section is where the discussion paper rejects ‘differentiation’. Instead, it endorses whole-class teaching alongside tiered interventions.
The term differentiation lacks a consistent definition or explanation in the literature, potentially leading to inconsistent understandings and applications in practice.

Since the publication of a systematic review on differentiation, conducted by its protagonists, that failed to find any positive evidence, the word seems to have been quietly dropped and the focus has shifted to Multi-Tiered Systems of Support

On the other hand, the mention of cognitive science is almost designed to provoke a backlash. I can already imagine the cries of ‘positivism’ and the obfuscatory arguments in response to the discussion paper.
